title: Ten, Five, Three, Two, Even One
hook: your community, or the one you're still looking for
carry: where people gather over torah, the shechinah rests
tomorrow: is "i don't know" allowed in a tradition full of answers?

segments.voice: Yesterday, we will do, and we will hear. Your practices. But a practice wants people around it, and that's today's question.

For two weeks after Owen's grandma died, someone from his church brought dinner every night. Noa noticed it, because when Mr. Levin died last spring, her synagogue did the same: a sign-up sheet, a casserole, a knock at the door. Two different houses of worship, one very familiar casserole. So what makes a group of people the place you belong?
screen: `DINNER EVERY NIGHT.` → `A SIGN-UP SHEET, A KNOCK.` → `WHAT MAKES IT BELONGING?`

segments.voice: Pirkei Avot has an answer that counts down. Rabbi Halafta of Kefar Hananiah taught: when ten sit together and busy themselves with Torah, the Shechinah, God's presence, rests among them. Then he goes lower. Five. Three. Two. Even one. Hillel adds the other side in a single line: do not separate yourself from the community. Here's a neighbor saying something close. Christians read in the Gospel of Matthew: "For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them." What's shared is real: a presence in the gathering, even a very small one, and a reason to show up. The honest difference matters too. In Matthew, Christians hear Jesus himself in the midst of those gathered in his name. In Avot, the gathering is around words of Torah, and the presence is the Shechinah. And some Jewish prayers, like Kaddish, wait for ten. Belonging, in both, isn't a crowd that already knows you. It's a table you keep coming back to. Something to tell a friend tonight: Avot counts all the way down to one.

segments.voice: Where you belong: the gathering you keep coming back to, where a presence rests, whether ten sit together or two.
Your line: where people gather over Torah, the Shechinah rests. Sometimes a full room, sometimes two people and a book. Shalom for now.

chat.says: owen says his church brought dinner every night. 'same as your synagogue, right?' is it the same?
options: Close: both find a presence in a small gathering. Different too: his says in Jesus' name.
Exactly the same. Every religion teaches the very same thing about community.
Not alike at all. His church is about belief; a synagogue is only about rules.
chat.meaning: Avot and Matthew both see a presence where a few gather. In Matthew it's Jesus; in Avot, the Shechinah over words of Torah.

tie.story: Rabbi Halafta taught that the Shechinah rests on ten who study Torah together, then counted down to five, three, two, even one.
tie.friend: Noa can tell Owen both houses see a presence in a small gathering: his in Jesus' name, hers over words of Torah.
tie.you: where do you keep coming back to?
